barber-state-readiness-check-chemistry-0.prompt: A virgin sodium-hydroxide relaxer is being applied to coarse, untreated hair. Where should the cream go first?

options.a: Midshaft and ends first, then the scalp last
options.b: The scalp first so body heat starts the process
options.c: The entire head at once to keep timing even
options.d: The nape only, then skip the crown later

barber-state-readiness-check-chemistry-0.explanation: Scalp heat speeds hydroxide processing, so the more resistant midshaft and ends are started first and the scalp last. Applying at the scalp first overprocesses the hair nearest the skin. A virgin application is timed as one service, not a nape-only shortcut.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses retouch logic with virgin application; scalp heat would overprocess that hair first.
distractorExplanations.c: One-pass coating ignores that scalp hair processes faster than the lengths.
distractorExplanations.d: The crown still needs the virgin application; skipping it leaves untreated texture.

barber-state-readiness-check-chemistry-0.prompt: A client wants oxidative color for typical gray coverage on a salt-and-pepper fade. Which developer strength matches NIC-level mixing?

options.a: 10-volume (3%) intended for three to four levels of lift
options.b: 20-volume (6%) as labeled for ordinary gray coverage
options.c: 40-volume (12%) brushed onto the scalp for deposit-only color
options.d: No developer; stir the tint with tap water instead

barber-state-readiness-check-chemistry-0.explanation: Standard oxidative gray coverage is mixed with 20-volume (about 6%) hydrogen peroxide unless the manufacturer specifies otherwise. Ten-volume is mainly deposit or tone with little lift. Forty-volume is a high-lift oxidizer and is not a scalp deposit-only developer. Water is not a substitute oxidizer.

distractorExplanations.a: 10-volume is deposit/tone chemistry; three-to-four-level lift is 30–40 volume territory.
distractorExplanations.c: 40-volume is high-lift and irritating on the scalp, not a deposit-only mixer.
distractorExplanations.d: Oxidative dyes need peroxide to develop; tap water leaves the color unoxidized.

barber-state-readiness-check-chemistry-0.prompt: Hair and scalp sit near pH 4.5–5.5. Why does a hydroxide relaxer swell the fiber and lift the cuticle so quickly?

options.a: It is acidic, like a neutralizing shampoo that closes the cuticle
options.b: It is pH-neutral, like a rinse-out conditioner left on the hair
options.c: It is highly alkaline (often pH 12–14), far above the acid mantle
options.d: Its low pH tightens the cuticle so product enters more slowly

barber-state-readiness-check-chemistry-0.explanation: Hydroxide relaxers are strongly alkaline, commonly around pH 12–14, while hair’s acid mantle is about 4.5–5.5. That pH jump swells the cortex and raises the cuticle so disulfide bonds can be broken (lanthionization). Acidic or neutral products do the opposite: they do not open the fiber for relaxing.

distractorExplanations.a: Neutralizing shampoos are acidic and used after rinsing to help close the cuticle, not to relax.
distractorExplanations.b: Conditioners are near-neutral cosmetics; they do not supply hydroxide alkalinity.
distractorExplanations.d: Low pH would compact the cuticle; relaxers work because they are high-pH, not low-pH.

barber-state-readiness-check-chemistry-0.prompt: A strand from a frequently colored fade feels dry, spongy, and drinks color in seconds. How should porosity change the chemical plan?

options.a: Treat it as resistant hair and double every processing time
options.b: Reach for 40-volume on every gray retouch to force lift
options.c: Assume a tightly closed cuticle like untreated virgin hair
options.d: Expect fast uptake and watch for overprocessing

barber-state-readiness-check-chemistry-0.explanation: High-porosity hair has a raised, damaged cuticle, so color and relaxer enter quickly and can overprocess or grab too dark. Lower volume, shorter timing, fillers, or a reconstructive pause are the usual controls. Resistant (low-porosity) hair is the opposite problem.

distractorExplanations.a: Doubling time on porous hair overprocesses; extra time is for low-porosity, resistant hair.
distractorExplanations.b: Higher volume on already porous hair increases breakage and scalp irritation.
distractorExplanations.c: A spongy, fast-drinking strand is open-cuticle porosity, not a closed virgin cuticle.

barber-state-readiness-check-chemistry-0.prompt: Before an aniline-derivative (oxidative) haircolor, when should a predisposition/patch test be read?

options.a: After the time on the label, commonly 24–48 hours
options.b: After about five minutes while the client is still in the chair
options.c: Only if the client already had a documented color allergy
options.d: After the full color is already processed on the scalp

barber-state-readiness-check-chemistry-0.explanation: A patch test (behind the ear or inner elbow) must sit for the manufacturer’s interval, typically 24–48 hours, so delayed allergic contact dermatitis can appear. A same-chair five-minute glance misses delayed reactions. The test is done before the service, not after color is already on the scalp, and first-time clients still need it when the label requires it.

distractorExplanations.b: Allergic contact reactions take hours; a five-minute chair read is too early.
distractorExplanations.c: Labels require a test before aniline color even without a prior known allergy.
distractorExplanations.d: A patch test is a pre-service screen; applying the full formula first is the exposure it is meant to prevent.

barber-state-readiness-check-chemistry-0.prompt: A client’s records show a sodium-hydroxide relaxer. He now wants an ammonium-thioglycolate perm on the same hair. What is the correct call?

options.a: Perm immediately with extra thio to even the pattern
options.b: Refuse thio on hydroxide-relaxed hair; they are incompatible
options.c: Blend a little hydroxide cream into the thio waving lotion
options.d: Apply thio only at the scalp line where new growth is soft

barber-state-readiness-check-chemistry-0.explanation: Hydroxide relaxing uses lanthionization and permanently alters disulfide bonds. Thio (perm or thio relaxer) on that hair causes extreme weakening and breakage. NIC teaching is that the two families are incompatible on the same fiber; do not mix products or ‘just do the new growth’ with the opposite chemistry.

distractorExplanations.a: Extra thio on hydroxide hair increases breakage; it does not repair the bond change.
distractorExplanations.c: Mixing hydroxide and thio creates an untested caustic blend and is a chemical-injury risk.
distractorExplanations.d: New growth next to hydroxide-treated lengths still overlaps at the junction and can snap.

barber-state-readiness-check-chemistry-0.prompt: Two minutes into a hydroxide relaxer the client reports a sharp scalp burn and the skin looks inflamed. What should the barber do first?

options.a: Leave the cream until the full timer ends, then rinse as usual
options.b: Spread more base cream over the burn and keep processing the timer
options.c: Rinse at once with tepid water using the maker’s emergency steps
options.d: Brush on neutralizer first without rinsing the relaxer off

barber-state-readiness-check-chemistry-0.explanation: A chemical burn is an emergency rinse, not a timing problem. Get the caustic cream off with plenty of tepid water and follow the manufacturer/SDS first-aid steps, then neutralizing shampoo if directed after the product is gone. Waiting, adding more base, or neutralizing on top of active relaxer keeps alkali on injured skin.

distractorExplanations.a: The timer does not override a burn; continued contact deepens the chemical injury.
distractorExplanations.b: Base cream is a pre-service scalp protectant; it cannot stop a burn already in progress.
distractorExplanations.d: Neutralizer on unrinsed hydroxide traps alkali on the scalp; a thorough water rinse comes first.

barber-state-readiness-check-chemistry-0.prompt: A client used a progressive metallic beard dye (or compound henna with metallic salts) and now wants a peroxide lightener. What is the risk?

options.a: Metallic dyes always rinse out in one shampoo, so bleach is safe
options.b: Mixing bleach into the leftover metallic dye will neutralize the metals
options.c: Metallic color only stains skin; the hair shaft cannot react with peroxide
options.d: Metals plus peroxide can heat, smoke, discolor, and snap the hair

barber-state-readiness-check-chemistry-0.explanation: Progressive dyes and compound (metallic) hennas deposit metal salts in the cortex. Hydrogen peroxide can oxidize those metals violently—heat, odd color, and breakage. Strand-test and, if metals are present, refuse oxidative lightener until the hair is free of that chemistry. Plant-only henna is a different product; ‘natural’ labels often hide metallic salts.

distractorExplanations.a: Metallic dyes are designed to build and stay; they do not wash out like a temporary rinse.
distractorExplanations.b: You cannot ‘neutralize’ metals by mixing bleach into the old dye; that is the dangerous reaction.
distractorExplanations.c: The salts sit in the fiber; the peroxide reaction is inside the hair, not only on skin.

barber-state-readiness-check-chemistry-0.prompt: A six-week hydroxide relaxer retouch is on the ticket. Where should the cream be limited?

options.a: New growth only, with no overlap onto already relaxed hair
options.b: Pulled through the ends on every visit to keep them straight
options.c: A double-thick coat on the previously relaxed midshaft
options.d: The ends only, leaving the new growth untreated this visit

barber-state-readiness-check-chemistry-0.explanation: A retouch processes virgin new growth. Overlapping hydroxide onto hair that is already lanthionized overprocesses and causes breakage at the old line of demarcation. Ends are not re-relaxed every visit; they may get a smoothing or conditioner only if the manufacturer allows, not a full-strength overlap.

distractorExplanations.b: Pulling relaxer through the ends each visit is a classic overlap-breakage error.
distractorExplanations.c: Extra product on already relaxed midshaft increases chemical damage, not control.
distractorExplanations.d: Skipping new growth leaves a band of untreated texture at the scalp, which is not a retouch.

barber-state-readiness-check-chemistry-0.prompt: When is 40-volume (12%) hydrogen peroxide the appropriate oxidizer in a barber color service?

options.a: For deposit-only gray blend mixed for the beard line
options.b: For labeled high-lift or off-scalp work, not routine scalp deposit
options.c: As a wound antiseptic after a nick during the color service
options.d: As the shop’s EPA-registered disinfectant for clipper blades

barber-state-readiness-check-chemistry-0.explanation: Forty-volume peroxide is a high-lift oxidizer (about three to four levels when the formula allows) and is generally kept off the scalp because of irritation and damage. Deposit-only and typical gray work use 10- or 20-volume. Developer is not first-aid peroxide and is not an EPA-registered disinfectant.

distractorExplanations.a: Deposit-only gray work uses 10-volume (or labeled low-volume), not 40-volume.
distractorExplanations.c: Color developer is far stronger than first-aid peroxide and is not for open skin.
distractorExplanations.d: Implements need an EPA-registered disinfectant; peroxide developer is a color oxidizer.

barber-state-readiness-check-chemistry-0.prompt: After rinsing an ammonium-thioglycolate (thio) relaxer, why is the oxidizing neutralizer required?

options.a: To break remaining disulfide bonds the thio cream left intact
options.b: To raise the hair’s pH still further so the cuticle stays open
options.c: To stop straightening and rebuild disulfide bonds in the new shape
options.d: To replace the water rinse, so a rinse step is optional

barber-state-readiness-check-chemistry-0.explanation: Thio reduces disulfide bonds so hair can be smoothed. The oxidizer (usually hydrogen peroxide or sodium bromate, as labeled) stops that reduction and rebuilds bonds in the straightened configuration. Skipping neutralization leaves hair weak and still processing. Water rinse removes product but does not re-form the bonds.

distractorExplanations.a: Bond breaking is the thio step; the neutralizer oxidizes to re-form bonds, not break more.
distractorExplanations.b: Neutralizers are not a second alkaline relaxer; the goal is to halt processing, not raise pH.
distractorExplanations.d: Manufacturer directions still require a thorough rinse; neutralizer is not a rinse substitute.

barber-state-readiness-check-chemistry-0.prompt: A client asks for aniline-derivative (coal-tar) tint on eyelashes or eyebrows. What is the legally and medically correct barber response?

options.a: Apply it after a negative patch test from the night before
options.b: Apply it if a petroleum barrier is first placed around the eye
options.c: Tint the brows only, because they sit farther from the globe
options.d: Refuse; FDA rules bar coal-tar dyes on lashes and brows

barber-state-readiness-check-chemistry-0.explanation: The FDA prohibits aniline/coal-tar hair dyes on eyelashes and eyebrows because of severe eye injury and blindness risk. A patch test, petroleum dam, or ‘brows only’ workaround does not make the product legal or safe in that location. Use only products labeled for the eye area, which oxidative haircolor is not.

distractorExplanations.a: A negative patch test does not override the FDA ban on aniline dye near the eyes.
distractorExplanations.b: A petroleum barrier does not prevent product from reaching the eye or mucosa.
distractorExplanations.c: The restriction covers eyebrows as well as lashes; distance from the globe is not a loophole.

barber-state-readiness-check-chemistry-0.prompt: A client says a home ‘no-lye’ relaxer was used last month and now wants a thio texture service. How should that history be treated?

options.a: No-lye means it was a thio cream, so another thio service is compatible
options.b: Treat no-lye as hydroxide chemistry; do not apply thio over it
options.c: No-lye products are pH-neutral conditioners and do not change the bonds
options.d: No-lye always rinses out in one shampoo, so thio may go on the same day

barber-state-readiness-check-chemistry-0.explanation: ‘No-lye’ in the relaxer aisle usually means calcium hydroxide activated with guanidine carbonate—not ammonium thioglycolate. It is still a hydroxide relaxer (lanthionization), just without sodium hydroxide. Thio waving or thio relaxing over it is the same incompatibility as thio over lye, so refuse overlapping services and strand-test any later chemical.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses marketing ‘no-lye’ with thio; no-lye is hydroxide, not ammonium thioglycolate.
distractorExplanations.c: No-lye relaxers are highly alkaline hydroxides, not pH-neutral conditioners.
distractorExplanations.d: Hydroxide relaxing is a permanent bond change; it does not shampoo out.

barber-state-readiness-check-chemistry-0.prompt: Before a full-head oxidative color on previously treated hair, why does the barber perform a strand test?

options.a: To replace the 24–48 hour skin patch test required for aniline dye
options.b: To decide whether gloves can be skipped for the remaining application
options.c: To preview timing, breakage, and result on a small section first
options.d: To heat the formula so 10-volume behaves like 40-volume developer

barber-state-readiness-check-chemistry-0.explanation: A strand test is a hair test: process a hidden section to judge porosity, timing, strength, and color before committing the whole head. It does not replace a skin predisposition test for aniline allergy, and it does not change PPE. Developer volume is mixed as labeled, not ‘heated up’ to mimic a stronger oxidizer.

distractorExplanations.a: Patch tests screen skin allergy; strand tests screen the hair. Both can be required.
distractorExplanations.b: Gloves remain PPE against repeated chemical exposure regardless of a strand result.
distractorExplanations.d: Heat does not convert 10-volume into 40-volume; oxidizer strength is the peroxide concentration.

barber-state-readiness-check-chemistry-0.prompt: A client wants a hydroxide relaxer and a high-lift bleach on the same hair in one appointment. What is the safe sequence?

options.a: Relax first, then bleach immediately while the cuticle is open
options.b: Bleach first, then relax the lightened hair to lock in the lift
options.c: Mix a little bleach into the relaxer to save a chair sitting
options.d: Skip stacking them the same day; wait and strand-test later

barber-state-readiness-check-chemistry-0.explanation: Relaxing and high-lift lightening on the same hair in one visit is an incompatible double chemical: two aggressive pH/oxidative assaults and a high breakage risk. NIC practice is to perform one chemical family, let the hair recover, then strand-test before any second service. Mixing products or stacking them ‘while the cuticle is open’ is how chemical burns and snap-off happen.

distractorExplanations.a: An open cuticle after relaxer makes bleach penetrate even more aggressively—breakage, not a shortcut.
distractorExplanations.b: Bleached hair is already weakened; a hydroxide relaxer on it commonly causes gummy, breaking fiber.
distractorExplanations.c: Combining bleach and relaxer in one bowl is an unlabeled caustic mixture and an injury risk.
